content:
I first heard about Iris a couple of years ago. When I first seriously tried to formalize a compiler analysis, I rejected Iris as the framework in which to formalize that work in a moment's thought. The reason was that I had my own functional language (which was not HeapLang) which came with a denotational semantics (and not a program logic based on an operational one) and I didn't need to reason about concurrency. So because Iris was sold as "the definitive program logic for higher order concurrency", I did not even bother looking at and understanding its base logic.

Years later, I now have successfully completed said formalization in terms of Iris' base logic, but only after multiple less successful efforts in other theorem provers/libraries. I think it would have helped me if Iris wasn't just sold as a giant monolith with a too narrow purpose.

Nudged by https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/490604-iris-lean/topic/Ordered.20Resource.20Algebras/near/619740948, I want to ask: would it make sense to break up Iris into separate libraries (maybe that's the case already) and give those libraries proper names (like BlueBell etc.) with motivating use cases? For example, I have used Iris' base logic to define a semantic domain for my denotational semantics and the logical relations it admits. I think that's huge! Hence "Iris' base logic" should have a separate name X, and the credit should be inverted, "X, which is the base logic Iris builds on".

Anyway, given the sheer amount of coordination involved with upstream Iris and the original authors, I'm not sure this is a realistic proposal. But I still think it would help selling Iris, even if it already sells well.

I also have to have the "I use Iris but not for concurrency" conversation a lot, lol. It's good to note this, but to be honest I do not think that splitting up the library is the solution to this problem.

There is a separate name for the general proof mode infrastructure: MoSeL. Not sure if there are also specific names for the other parts.
The repository is already split up into different folders for the different parts, so one can already use them individually. Not sure if there is a good way to advertise this.

I also have to have the "I use Iris but not for concurrency" conversation a lot, lol.

I think the only part of Iris that has something to do with concurrency is the requirement for invariants to be open only during an atomic step. Everything else is just a consequence of separation logic itself: separation is naturally friendly to concurrency.

Aside of the Heaplang and the proof mode it's not clear what one would like to split out of Iris.

I should also say that I think Sebastian raises a good point and I've had conversations before where I had to explain to people that Iris is more than just a separation logic for HeapLang. I am just not sure how to best advertise what Iris Lean has to offer. Maybe one could make it more explicit in the README of the repo?
